analysis:
The change is a single added test file (provider-swift/Tests/DarkbloomCLITests/SandboxWorkDiskTests.swift, lines 1-433). It adds no production code, so it creates no new attack surface and weakens no existing control. I examined every test against TB-013/T-061 (the CLI downloads and runs the sandbox add-on's installer as the Mac owner) and TB-012/A-019.

What the tests document about the unseen production behavior:
- `--disk` paths are normalized to absolute paths and an empty value is refused (lines 25-36).
- The installer arguments are passed through as discrete argv elements, so there is no shell injection (lines 38-47).
- The ownership fix command single-quotes mount points containing spaces or apostrophes (lines 80-82). The `sudo diskutil enableOwnership` command is shown to the owner and run only after a [y/N] consent at an interactive prompt (lines 360-389).
- `runInForeground` and `enableOwnership` do nothing when no terminal is in the foreground (lines 149-157). This is a good control.
- Setup stops before any download when the work disk fails the check (lines 187-209, 391-412).
- Setup refuses `--disk` when the downloaded installer does not advertise support for it (lines 211-234).
- Candidate drives are restricted to local, writable, APFS, Finder-visible volumes mounted at their own /Volumes/<name> (lines 100-137).

The concerns I considered are all in production code outside this PR. They are the quoting implementation, the real `sudo` invocation, and whether the installer is integrity-verified (T-061). None can be assessed from this tests-only diff.

The threat model could gain a note that `--disk` has the CLI run `sudo diskutil` for the owner. The production SandboxWorkDisk source should be reviewed for that. I do not claim the SandboxWorkDisk implementation is secure.
